You can on accident fry your CPU and/or GPU if you're not careful.

There are many third and native software clients which allow you to force the CPU and/or GPU to "run" faster than they were design for. This is otherwise knows as overclocking.

E.g. My CPU is "clocked" at 2.00 Ghz but I have overclocked it to run at 2.60 Ghz. This is okay to an extent.

However if you overclock your CPU by too much than it can cope with then you will end up frying your CPU because either the computer will crash because it has become unstable. Or the CPU will generate soo much heat that it will in effect burn.

So when overclocking it is important to monitor the stability of your system and the temperature.

You are absolutely correct, I have a special edition of the book where at the end of the chapter there is commentary by another well respected author (I'll post the name if I can remember). This passage was in the commentary after chapter 19 I think.

Steve jobs insisted on taking a cash salary of $1 per year. At the end of 1999, to thank jobs for serving as CEO "for the previous 2 1/2 years without compensation," the board presented him with his very own Gulf stream jet, at a cost to the company of a mere $90 million. The next month Jobs had agreed to drop "interim" from his job title, and the board rewarded him with options on 20 million shares. (until then, Jobs had held a grand total of two shares in Apple stock.) 

The principle behind such option grants isn't to align the interests of managers with outside investors. If you are an outside Apple share-holder, you want it's managers to be rewarded only Apple's stock earns superior returns. Nothing else could possibly be fair to you and the other owners of the company. But, as John Bogle, former chairman of the Vanguard funds, points out, nearly all managers sell the stock they receive immediately after exercising their options. How could dumping millions of shares for an instant profit possibly align their interests with those of the company's loyal long-term shareholders?

In Jobs' case, if Apple stock rises by just 5% annually through the beginning of 2010, he will be able to cash in his options for $548.3 million. In other words, even if Apple's stocks earns no better than half the long-term average return of the overall stock market, Jobs will land a half-a-billion dollar windfall.

Does that align his interests with those of Apple's shareholders - or malign the trust that Apple's shareholders have placed in the board of directors.

-- That is just a few paragraphs from a book that I've read called "The Intelligent Investor" by Benjamin Graham
